title: Two Sum
summary: Find two indices whose values add up to `target`. Instead of checking every pair, walk the array once and remember each value's index in a hash map; for each number you only need to ask whether its complement `target - x` has already appeared.

complexity.note: Best case is when the first two numbers are the pair. The map can grow to n entries.

intuition: For each `nums[i]`, the only partner that works is `need = target - nums[i]`.
A hash map from value to index answers "have I seen `need`?" in O(1).
Check the map before inserting `nums[i]`, so an element never pairs with itself.
One pass is enough: when the second element of the pair arrives, the first is already in the map.
pitfalls: Inserting before checking lets `[3, 2, 4], target = 6` return `[0, 0]` (using 3 twice).
Sorting first loses the original indices unless you carry them along.
The brute-force double loop is O(n²); interviewers expect the hash map version.
Returning values instead of indices.

steps.explain: 2 was seen at index 0, so `nums[0] + nums[1] = 9`.

title: Valid Anagram
summary: Two strings are anagrams when they use exactly the same letters the same number of times. Count letters of `s` up and letters of `t` down in one array of 26 counters; they are anagrams only if every counter ends at zero.

complexity.note: Best case is a length mismatch. The 26 counters are constant space.

intuition: Different lengths can never be anagrams, so check that first.
One pass: `count[s[i]]++` and `count[t[i]]--` together.
If any counter is non-zero at the end, some letter is over- or under-used.
An int[26] beats a HashMap for lowercase letters: faster and simpler.
pitfalls: Forgetting the length check, then reading past the end of the shorter string.
`c - 'a'` breaks on uppercase or Unicode; use a HashMap<Character, Integer> for the follow-up.
Sorting both strings works but is O(n log n).

title: Contains Duplicate
summary: Return true if any value appears at least twice. Add each value to a hash set; `add` returns false the moment a value is already there.

complexity.note: Best case is a duplicate in the first two elements. The set can hold all n values.

intuition: A HashSet answers "seen before?" in O(1).
`set.add(x)` returns false if x was already present, so check and insert in one call.
Stop at the first duplicate; no need to finish the scan.
pitfalls: Sorting and comparing neighbours is O(n log n) and mutates the input.
Comparing every pair is O(n²) and times out.

title: Majority Element
summary: Find the value that appears more than n/2 times. Boyer–Moore voting keeps one candidate and a counter: matching values vote for it, others vote against, and when the counter hits zero a new candidate takes over. The true majority always survives.

complexity.note: Always one full pass with two variables.

intuition: Pair each majority element with a different element and cancel them; the majority still has some left over.
`count == 0` means everything so far cancelled out, so start fresh with the current value.
The final candidate is the majority, as long as one is guaranteed to exist.
pitfalls: Without the guarantee, the survivor might not be a majority; verify with a second pass.
Changing the candidate when count is 1 instead of 0.
A HashMap of counts works but uses O(n) space; interviewers ask for O(1).

title: Group Anagrams
summary: Group words that are anagrams of each other. Sorting a word's letters gives a key that all its anagrams share, so a map from sorted key to list of words collects the groups in one pass.

complexity.note: n words of length up to k. A 26-count key makes it O(n·k).

intuition: Anagrams become identical after sorting their letters: "eat", "tea", "ate" → "aet".
Use that sorted string as a HashMap key; the value is the list of words in that group.
`computeIfAbsent` creates the list the first time a key appears.
pitfalls: Using `char[]` directly as the key: arrays use identity hashing, so nothing groups.
Building the count-key as "1112" without separators can collide; use '#' between counts.
Assuming the output order matters; any order is accepted.

title: Top K Frequent Elements
summary: Return the k most frequent values. Count frequencies with a map, then place each value into a bucket indexed by its frequency. Reading buckets from the highest frequency down gives the answer in O(n), no sorting needed.

complexity.note: A frequency can be at most n, so there are n + 1 buckets.

intuition: Frequencies are bounded by n, so they can be used as array indices.
`bucket[f]` holds every value that appears exactly f times.
Walk buckets from n down to 1 and collect values until you have k.
pitfalls: Sorting the map entries by count is O(n log n), fine but not optimal.
A min-heap of size k is O(n log k); know both and when each is better.
Sizing the bucket array as n instead of n + 1 crashes when every element is equal.

title: Product of Array Except Self
category: Arrays & Hashing · Prefix and suffix products
summary: For each index, return the product of every other element, without division. The answer at i is (product of everything left of i) × (product of everything right of i): fill left products in one pass, then multiply in right products in a second pass.

complexity.note: Two passes. The output array doesn't count as extra space, and the suffix is one variable.

intuition: `res[i] = prefix(i) × suffix(i)`, where neither includes `nums[i]`.
First pass: `res[i] = res[i-1] × nums[i-1]` stores prefix products.
Second pass right-to-left: keep a running `suffix` and multiply it in.
No division means zeros need no special handling.
pitfalls: Using division breaks on zeros, and the problem forbids it anyway.
Off-by-one: the prefix for index 0 is 1 (empty product), not nums[0].
Updating `suffix` before multiplying includes `nums[i]` in its own answer.

steps.title: Prefix product
steps.explain: `res[1] = res[0] × nums[0] = 1 × 1 = 1`: the product of everything left of 1.

steps.explain: `res[2] = res[1] × nums[1] = 1 × 2 = 2`: the product of everything left of 2.

steps.title: Prefix product
steps.explain: `res[3] = res[2] × nums[2] = 2 × 3 = 6`: the product of everything left of 3.

steps.title: Multiply in the suffix

steps.explain: `suffix = 24` is the product of everything right of 0. `res[0]` becomes 24.

steps.title: Done
steps.explain: Each `res[i]` is prefix × suffix, never including `nums[i]` itself.

title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
summary: Find the length of the longest run of consecutive integers, in O(n). Put all values in a set. A value starts a run only if `x - 1` is absent; from each start, count upward while `x + len` exists. Each number is visited at most twice, so the total is linear.

complexity.note: The inner while only runs from run starts, so every value is extended over at most once.

intuition: Only begin counting at a number whose predecessor is missing; that's the start of a run.
From a start, walk `x+1, x+2, …` using O(1) set lookups.
Iterating over the set (not the array) skips duplicates for free.
pitfalls: Starting a count from every number makes it O(n²).
Sorting is O(n log n), which the problem rules out.
Forgetting the empty-array case (answer 0).
